text:
Recent work separates persistent preferences, immediate intent, and multiple concurrent interests. MSMT-LSI (2024) combines temporal embeddings with separate long/short-term attention networks; LS4SRec (2025) uses independent interest encoders plus collaborative graph signals. These support testing distinct historical and recent-context representations rather than relying exclusively on SASRec’s final state. [MSMT-LSI](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-024-00460-5), [LS4SRec](https://doi.org/10.1145/3723173). Multi-interest temporal modeling also explicitly distinguishes enduring preferences from brief interests with little subsequent purchase intent, using interest subgraphs, temporal modules, and contrastive separation. [Ma et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.knosys.2024.112657). S²HyRec (2026) similarly distinguishes global intent tendencies from temporal contextual intent. [S²HyRec](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/38566).

HyperHawkes (WWW 2025) is especially relevant to recurring needs: latent intent clustering, temporal Hawkes processes for repeated intent, and attention mixtures for short-term changes. Repeated intent can span different items, making it relevant when recommendations exclude previously consumed products. [Paper](https://pintonos.github.io/publication/peintner-www-2025/peintner-www-2025.pdf). Lightweight adaptation hypothesis: retain SASRec, add pooled historical preferences and several recent-window interest vectors, then gate their contributions using observed inter-event gaps and candidate compatibility. Compare against simple recency pooling before introducing graphs or clustering. Validate each category and select by macro HR@10; these papers do not establish gains on the pinned benchmark. Treat satisfied needs and complementary purchases as hypotheses inferred from transitions, not observed labels: interaction histories alone cannot reliably distinguish satisfaction, abandonment, and intent switching.
